name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,793

clue.text: Old fart in Blur seen with Rear of the Year (5)

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: a fog is a blur
last letter of 'the'
Y is the standard abbreviation for year

annotation.surface: An ageing member of the band Blur turning up at the Rear of the Year awards.
annotation.walkthrough: Rear of the Year is a British award for the best-looking bottom; here 'Rear of' simply takes the last letter of 'the', and Year shrinks to Y.
annotation.definitionFit: A fogey is a fussy old-fashioned person, which is what 'old fart' means in slang.

clue.text: Fellow criminal hoary and old as Hoskins? (9)

definitions.note: 'as Hoskins' stands in for an adjective: the setter calls himself foolhardy

indicators.note: criminal letters are crooked, out of their lawful order

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
HOARY + OLD rearranged

annotation.surface: A villainous accomplice, white-haired and aged, compared to the setter himself.
annotation.walkthrough: Hoskins is this puzzle's setter, so 'as Hoskins' is a self-mocking definition: rash, like the setter. 'and' only joins the two halves of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: The setter is teasing himself as reckless, which is what foolhardy means.

clue.text: German drug rubbish? Bother! (3,2)

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for German
E is ecstasy
tat is cheap junk

annotation.surface: Someone dismisses a German drug as rubbish and then shrugs it off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bother!' reads as an exclamation of annoyance, but it is the verb: to get at someone is to nag or bother them.
annotation.definitionFit: To get at someone is to criticise or pester them, to bother them.

clue.text: Those providing cover for some privates? (1-6)

definitions.text: Those providing cover for some privates?

blocks.note: sounds like soldiers giving covering fire; really garments that cover up
sounds like army privates; really the private parts, and only men's

annotation.surface: Soldiers giving covering fire to a group of army privates.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Privates' and 'cover' sound military, but the privates are private parts; Y-fronts are British men's briefs with a Y-shaped front seam.
annotation.definitionFit: Y-fronts are underpants, which cover a man's privates.

clue.text: Forum contributor drinking port is an arse (9)

indicators.note: one thing drinking another takes it inside

blocks.note: someone who posts on an internet forum
Rio de Janeiro, the Brazilian port

annotation.surface: An insult hurled at a forum regular who drinks port.
annotation.walkthrough: 'port' tempts you toward the wine; it is a harbour city, Rio. The insult 'is an arse' turns out to be literal.
annotation.definitionFit: The posterior is the backside, a polite word for an arse.

clue.text: Contract to appear in Palladium tickled Pink (7)

indicators.note: one thing appearing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: Pd is the chemical symbol for palladium
a lease is a rental contract

annotation.surface: The singer Pink delighted to be signed for a show at the London Palladium.
annotation.walkthrough: The Palladium is a London theatre and Pink a pop singer, but here Palladium is the element and 'tickled pink' means delighted.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to be tickled pink is to be delighted, flushed with pleasure.

clue.text: Jets circling seventh of offshore wind generators? (7)

indicators.note: the outer word circles, going round the letter
take the seventh letter of the next word

blocks.note: spouts are jets of liquid
O-F-F-S-H-O-R: the seventh letter is R

annotation.surface: Water jets around offshore wind turbines.
annotation.walkthrough: Offshore wind farms prime you for turbines; the wind here is flatulence, which Brussels sprouts are notorious for causing.
annotation.definitionFit: Brussels sprouts famously give people wind, so they generate it.

clue.text: Family member removing top in high spirits (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue the top of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a relation is a family member

annotation.surface: A relative taking their top off while in a merry mood.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone undressing at a party; 'top' is the first letter of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the joyful lift of mood called elation is being in high spirits.

clue.text: It messes around with a man or a lover (9)

indicators.note: letters messed around are jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder joined by 'with'

annotation.surface: Someone fooling around with a man or with a lover.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder ends mid-phrase: 'a man or a' supplies the letters, so the 'or a' that reads as a choice is part of it.
annotation.definitionFit: Borrowed from Italian, where innamorata means a woman in love: a sweetheart or mistress.

clue.text: Gas constant? Age going up? Relax! (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up reads the letters bottom to top

blocks.note: R is the universal gas constant in physics
an age is a period of TIME, read upward

annotation.surface: Three terse physics-lab exclamations ending in an order to calm down.
annotation.walkthrough: Remit's older sense is to slacken or ease off, as a fever remits.
annotation.definitionFit: To remit is to ease or relax, as when effort or pain lessens.

clue.text: Openly gay don pinching contrary soldier’s sweaters? (9)

indicators.note: the outer words pinch the piece, holding it inside
contrary means the other way round

blocks.note: out = openly gay
RE (Royal Engineers) turned round
to don is to put on, to wear

annotation.surface: A gay university lecturer stealing a soldier's jumpers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'don' looks like a university lecturer but is the verb to put on; sweaters are an example of outerwear, hence the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: Sweaters are garments worn over others, an example of outerwear.

clue.text: A large member can create apprehension (5)

blocks.note: as printed
L = large, as on clothes labels
an arm is a limb, a member of the body

annotation.surface: A saucy line about a well-endowed man causing nervousness.
annotation.walkthrough: In this puzzle's cheeky register 'large member' invites a rude reading; it is just L and ARM.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the sudden worry that something bad is coming is both alarm and apprehension.

clue.text: Chat up American in drag at work (3,2)

blocks.note: in American slang a hit is a drag on a cigarette or joint
on = working, as a machine is on

annotation.surface: An American in women's clothing flirting with someone at the office.
annotation.walkthrough: 'in drag' suggests cross-dressing, but drag is a puff of smoke, which Americans call a hit.
annotation.definitionFit: Two informal idioms for making a romantic pass at someone, the American one and the British one.

clue.text: I tug lout's pants in fight for supremacy (4,2,3)

indicators.note: British slang for rubbish, so the letters are a rubbish arrangement to be fixed

blocks.note: anagram fodder

annotation.surface: Two people wrestling over a yob's trousers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'pants' reads as trousers being tugged; it is the British slang adjective for rubbish, telling you to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: To slug it out is to fight hard until one side wins.

clue.text: Rubbish bit of drugs ... just said no? (7)

indicators.note: a bit of a word here is its first letter

blocks.note: refuse is rubbish
first letter of drugs

annotation.surface: Echoing the anti-drug slogan Just Say No.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface borrows the 1980s anti-drugs slogan 'Just say no'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense, with the question mark nodding at the anti-drug slogan.

clue.text: Dead fast to skirt round unionist emitting gas (9)

indicators.note: the outer words skirt round, enclosing the letter

blocks.note: flat = dead, as a flat battery or drink
U is the abbreviation for Unionist
Lent is the Christian fast

annotation.surface: A dash to avoid a politician who is breaking wind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dead fast' reads as one phrase meaning very quick, but dead and fast are separate words that split apart to hold the unionist.
annotation.definitionFit: Flatulent means suffering from or passing wind.

clue.text: Star that's hit Tanner? (7)

blocks.note: the sun is a star
to lamp someone is British slang for hitting them

annotation.surface: A celebrity punching someone called Tanner.
annotation.walkthrough: A tanner is also an old sixpence coin; here it is something that tans you. To lamp someone is British slang for punching them.
annotation.definitionFit: A crossword-style coinage: a tanner is anything that tans you, and an ultraviolet lamp does.

clue.text: Getting high? Spice hit at noon helps! (7,2)

indicators.note: letters that get high are intoxicated and jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder
N is the abbreviation for noon

annotation.surface: A drug user swears that a lunchtime dose of Spice gets them through.
annotation.walkthrough: Spice is a synthetic cannabis drug in Britain, so the surface is a stoner's endorsement.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to pitch in is to join in and lend a hand.

clue.text: 365 days with knight essentially seems scarily longer! (7)

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its middle letter

blocks.note: a year has 365 days
N is the knight in chess notation
middle letter of s-e-E-m-s
middle letter of s-c-a-R-i-l-y

annotation.surface: A year with a knight feels frighteningly long.
annotation.walkthrough: 'longer' reads as 'more long', but it is someone who longs.
annotation.definitionFit: A yearner is one who yearns, or longs: a longer.

clue.text: Rhino saved for the next generation? (4,3)

definitions.text: Rhino saved for the next generation?

blocks.note: sounds like conservation of the animal; really money put by, rhino being old slang for cash
sounds like our grandchildren; really the chick in a bird's egg

annotation.surface: Conservationists protecting the rhinoceros for future generations.
annotation.walkthrough: Rhino is old British slang for money, not the animal; the next generation is the chick in the egg.
annotation.definitionFit: A nest egg is a sum of money saved for the future.

clue.text: Old clothes split without intention (7)

indicators.note: in its old sense of outside: the word goes outside the other

blocks.note: a rent is a tear, a split
an aim is an intention

annotation.surface: Worn clothes that tore without anyone meaning them to.
annotation.walkthrough: 'without' reads as 'lacking', as in torn without meaning to be; here it has its old sense of outside. 'Old' marks the answer as an old-fashioned word.
annotation.definitionFit: Raiment is an archaic word for clothing.

clue.text: V&A worker grabbing Greek's bum (7)

indicators.note: the outer letters grab the piece, holding it inside

blocks.note: the ampersand is dropped
Gr is the abbreviation for Greek; the 's just joins it to what follows
the worker ant

annotation.surface: A museum employee groping a Greek visitor's backside.
annotation.walkthrough: The V&A is London's Victoria and Albert Museum. 'bum' is the American sense, a tramp, not the British bottom.
annotation.definitionFit: An American sense: a bum is a tramp or down-and-out, not the British backside.

clue.text: Six royals and two Norsemen? (7)

blocks.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
kings are royals

annotation.surface: A head count of six monarchs plus two Scandinavian raiders.
annotation.walkthrough: 'and two' signals that the same letters carry two readings: VI KINGS is six royals, VIKINGS the Norsemen.
annotation.definitionFit: The Vikings were the Norse seafaring raiders.

clue.text: Guy with gangster stealing one of the crown jewels? (7)

indicators.note: the outer word steals the piece, taking it inside

blocks.note: a gent is a man, a guy
I is the Roman numeral one
Al Capone, the archetypal gangster

annotation.surface: A man and a mobster pinching one of the Crown Jewels from the Tower.
annotation.walkthrough: The Crown Jewels are the royal regalia in the Tower of London; 'the crown jewels' is also slang for a man's privates. Only the guy does the stealing; the gangster tags on after.
annotation.definitionFit: Genital means relating to the genitals, jokingly called the crown jewels.

clue.text: Cook trims duck and piece of chicken (9)

indicators.note: cooking the letters mixes them up

blocks.note: anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A chef trimming a duck and a chicken piece.
annotation.walkthrough: The kitchen scene makes 'Cook' look like the chef; it is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A cook's name for a cut: the lower leg of a bird, shaped like the stick used to beat a drum.

clue.text: Dunces primarily sent up Hoskins's often blue material? (5)

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the word gives its first letter
in a down clue, sent up reads the letters upward

blocks.note: first letter of dunces
the setter speaking: Hoskins's = MINE, read upward

annotation.surface: Fools mocking the setter's usual smutty material.
annotation.walkthrough: 'blue material' pretends to be the setter's rude jokes; it is fabric. Hoskins is the setter, so his is MINE.
annotation.definitionFit: Denim is a cotton fabric, usually dyed blue.

clue.text: City pub importing drop of Maltese spirit (5)

indicators.note: the outer letters import the piece, bringing it inside
a drop of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: New York
first letter of Maltese
PH = public house, as on maps

annotation.surface: A city bar bringing in a shot of Maltese liquor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'drop' and 'spirit' suggest a drink; the spirit is a nature sprite from myth.
annotation.definitionFit: A nymph is a nature spirit in Greek myth.

clue.text: Oscar-winning film is a bit wet (5)

indicators.note: the film wins the Oscar, taking it inside

blocks.note: a mist is a thin film, as on glass
O is Oscar in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: A critic dismissing an Academy Award winner as rather drippy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Oscar-winning film' reads as a movie; it is a mist that has won the letter O.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: damp but not soaked, which is what 'a bit wet' describes.

clue.text: Resort in which you'll find English relative (5)

indicators.note: the resort is the place in which the letter is found

blocks.note: Nice, the French Riviera resort
E = English

annotation.surface: A holiday town where you'll meet an English relation.
annotation.walkthrough: Nice is a proper noun here, the French Riviera resort, hiding behind the capital letter at the start of the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a sibling's daughter is one kind of relative.

clue.text: It's seen in drunken brainiacs (9)

indicators.note: drunken letters stagger out of order

blocks.note: anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A remark that clever people also get drunk.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is the opening phrase, which reads as ordinary grammar rather than letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An Einstein is a genius, a brainiac, after the physicist.

clue.text: Uni crowds welcoming independent moderates (9)

indicators.note: the outer words welcome the letter in

blocks.note: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
I = independent
a gate is the attendance at a sports match

annotation.surface: Students welcoming a politically independent speaker.
annotation.walkthrough: 'moderates' looks like a noun for centrists, fitting the political surface; it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: To mitigate is to moderate or lessen something.

clue.text: Some foul, at intervals, language (5)

indicators.note: some of the words: the answer is part of them

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word, through the second, into the start of the third

annotation.surface: Someone swearing in fits and starts.
annotation.walkthrough: 'at intervals' looks like an alternate-letters instruction, but the answer runs straight through 'foul, at in-'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the tongue of ancient Rome is one language among many.
